note: testRenderI: execute("render -n D=12,F=34 -p nec1") then assertEquals against this string -- a byte-exact assertion. S defaults to 255-D = 243 per the IRP's S:0..255=255-D; the carrier is the IRP's 38.4k.
testToIrSignalNec1 with NameEngine {D=12,S=34,F=56}. That test asserts approximate equality only, but the string is published, and the same one is IrScrutinizer's NEC1_PRONTO in GuiMainNGTest.java.

A decodePrint() input in Decoder.main(), removed in f94d9ea2. The parameters are not stated beside it; IrpTransmogrifier decodes it as Sony20 {D=12,S=34,F=56}. Weaker than an assertion for that reason, which is why Sony20 also carries the MakeHex sweep below.

No published NECx2 vector with stated parameters was found. This is generated by a pinned release, which also reproduces both published NEC1 strings above exactly. D=7,S=7 is the BN59-01199F's address. IrpTransmogrifier's NECx2 carrier is 38.4k (DecodeIR says 38.0k).

MakeHex's own shipped Sony20 definition, with only the Device line changed to the RMT-B118P's 26.226. That build reproduces a MakeHex output published on RemoteCentral in 2013 byte for byte. MakeHex rounds against the word's period, as D6 rule 4 does, so our bytes match on 127 of 128 functions. F=127 differs in its lead-out word alone, and only because MakeHex rounds each pair cumulatively.

The constant RC5_1_1_0 in ShortProntoNGTest, which long2short collapses to the same short code as RC5_1_1_1 below. The name gives D=1, F=1 and the toggle state; the frame was decoded to check it. The lead-out is the only word our D6 rounding spells differently.
RC5_1_1_1 in ShortProntoNGTest: the same command with the toggle bit set. Together with the T=0 vector it pins both states of T, which is the one field a remote file cannot set (DESIGN D3b).

testDecodeRc5: decode --strict -p rc5 on this string must give RC5: {D=7,F=5}. A decode assertion, not a render one, so the parameters are the tool's own answer; T=0 is what our encoder must use to reproduce it. A different address and command from D=1, F=1, so it pins the field bit order.

testDecodePioneer: a Pronto string at 40 kHz that the test asserts decodes as Pioneer and, at a 2000 Hz frequency tolerance, as NEC2 (L185; not at 1000, L190). Pioneer is NEC2 at 40k (IrpProtocols.xml: 'distinguished from NEC2 only by frequency'). The parameters are not stated beside the string: the 1.2.14 release decodes it as Pioneer {D=90,F=38} and its `render -n D=90,F=38 -p pioneer` reproduces it byte for byte; S defaults to 255-D = 165. That release's `decode` does not list NEC2 for it, so the NEC2 half of the assertion belongs to the pinned commit's library and was not re-run here. Weaker than a render assertion for that reason, which is why NEC2 also carries the 38.4k render below. Our bytes differ at nearly every word: 564 us is 22.5 cycles at 40 kHz and the two rounding rules split the half differently.

Generated by the pinned release, not found in print: the same release that reproduces both published NEC1 strings exactly. D=12,S=34,F=56 are the parameters of the published NEC1 vector, so the frame is directly comparable with it; at the IRP's own 38.4k, with the whole frame in the repeat slot.

No published NECx1 vector with stated parameters was found (IrpTransmogrifier's tests at c945e76 carry NECx1 only as a decode expectation for a hardware capture, which the structural vector uses). Generated by the pinned release. D is even, so the repeat frame's bit ~D:1 is a one (1,-3): pinned by this vector and, for D=44, by the capture.

The same parameters as the vector above with D odd, so the repeat frame's bit ~D:1 is a zero (1,-1). Together they pin both polarities of the one field NECx1 adds to NECx2; the capture shows only the even case.

Girr's reference command set for protocol sony12 with D=1: the command power_toggle, F=21, with its ccf. Parameters are stated beside the string, but all 25 of its commands match IrpTransmogrifier's rendering word for word, so it is evidently that tool's output committed to a sibling repository: published, not independent of the tool. The frame is Sony's well-known TV power code, 0xA90 written in transmission order. The lead-out is the only word our D6 rounding spells differently.

Generated by the pinned release. D=23 F=70 is the first capture in IrpTransmogrifier's own teaser set (Sony12B.ict), whose durations the encoder also reproduces; neither value is symmetric, so unlike D=1 this pins the field order and both bit orders.

No published Sony15 string has the ^45m lead-out. This render is generated by the pinned release at the parameters of the one published Sony15 string (IrpTransmogrifierNGTest testDecodeSony15, tests/vectors/sirc-structural.json), and its pairs are identical to that string's apart from the header split and the lead-out word.

testToIrSignalRc6: rc6.toIrSignal with NameEngine {D=12,F=34} must approximately equal this string, so the parameters are stated beside it. The assertion is approximate, not byte-exact, like NEC1's second vector; the string is nonetheless exactly what the 1.2.14 release renders for D=12,F=34 (T defaults to 0). Ends on a mark, so the 107 ms extent is a separate gap word, which is the only word our D6 rounding spells differently.

The constant RC6_1_3 in ShortProntoNGTest, which long2short collapses to a short code and ShortPronto.parse expands back, both asserted. The name gives D=1, F=3; the frame was decoded to check it and to find T=0. A last command bit of 1 ends the frame on a space, so the 107 ms extent lengthens it, an ending the D=12 F=34 vector above does not exercise. The lead-out is the only word our D6 rounding spells differently.

No published RCA-38 Pronto string with stated parameters was found in IrpTransmogrifier's tests (its only RCA-38 data is the RCA-38.ict capture and RCA-38.exp expected decodes, which gate 2a uses). D=15, F=144 is the capture's Aspect key. Generated by a pinned release, which also reproduces the published RC6 strings above exactly. Our bytes differ at the lead-in only: 3680 us is 0x8E cycles at the nominal carrier and 0x8F at the word's period.

No published Thomson7 Pronto string was found (IrpTransmogrifier's Thomson-0625 capture and its expected decodes are what gate 2a uses). D=12, F=74 is that capture's Vol+ key, with T=0 as the ledger compiles it. T=1 was passed over deliberately: with an even number of 1 bits the gap is an exact half cycle (34,500 us x 33 kHz = 1138.5), which the tool's double arithmetic rounds down and the decimal half-up rule in reference_quantizers.py rounds up. D=12, F=74, T=0 has five 1 bits and no tie. Our bytes differ in 19 words because 500 us is 16.5 cycles at the nominal carrier (0x11) and 16.45 at the word's period (0x10).

No published Pioneer-2Part render or assertion exists in IrpTransmogrifier's tests (its only Pioneer assertion, DecoderNGTest.testDecodePioneer, is a decode of one plain-Pioneer frame). This is generated by the pinned release; D0=170,F0=91,D=175,F=36 is the Setup key IrpTransmogrifier's own PioneerMix2.exp decodes from a real Pioneer receiver. At 40 kHz a 564 us unit is 22.56 cycles, which our word-period rule (D6 rule 4) rounds to 22 and the nominal-carrier rule to 23, so our bytes differ from the tool's in 201 of 208 words: the lead-in mark and every bit mark and space (the 8-unit lead-in space and both lead-out gaps agree). The timings themselves are identical under the tool's own rule.

No published JVC render or assertion exists in IrpTransmogrifier's tests. This is generated by the pinned release; D=5,F=19 is one of the published decodes in its JVC.exp. Our bytes differ from it in three words: the lead-in mark (word 4) and the two lead-out gaps (words 39 and 73), by 1, 3 and 4 cycles: the frequency word 006D implies a 38.03 kHz period against the 37.9 kHz the tool rounds by (0.35%).

No published Sharp render or assertion exists in IrpTransmogrifier's tests. This is generated by the pinned release; D=1,F=22 is the Power code its Sharp_Pronto.exp decodes from a Sharp remote's Pronto export. Our bytes differ from it only in the three lead-out words, by 1 to 2 cycles.

No published Denon render or assertion with the registered (^67m) IRP exists: ShortProntoNGTest's DENON string is the superseded form with fixed 43,560 us gaps, so it cannot serve as a gate 2b timing vector, and is used only as a structural citation. This is generated by the pinned release; D=8,F=175 is the 'left' key its Denon_left.exp decodes from a Denon receiver. Our bytes differ from it only in the three lead-out words, by 1 to 2 cycles.

Up on the Samsung Blu-ray remote whose capture IrpTransmogrifier's own test data holds (Samsung36.exp: Up decodes as Samsung36 {D=32,S=0,F=24,E=7}). `function` is the ledger's E:F packing, 7*256 + 24 = 1816. No Pronto string for Samsung36 is published, so this is a render of the pinned release; the same parameters are what the DB's UP key (hex 0400E18) maps to.

Every field different (D=0x12, S=0x34, E=5, F=0x56), so a swapped D and S, a wrong bit order or a misplaced E nibble cannot pass. `function` = 5*256 + 86 = 1366. A render of the pinned release, like its sibling; nothing published to compare it with.
Key 1 of the Proton remote whose capture IrpTransmogrifier's test data holds (Proton.exp: Proton {D=20,F=1}). A render of the pinned release; no Pronto string for Proton is published.

D=0x12, F=0x35: every bit of both bytes in play and the two different, so swapped bytes or reversed bit order cannot pass. Chosen so that no duration lands exactly half-way between two cycle counts (see NOTES/misc.md on tests/reference_quantizers.py).
Close on the strict-F12 remote whose capture IrpTransmogrifier's test data holds (F12.exp: F12 {D=0,S=1,F=16}); the frame is the same as F12_relaxed's. A render of the pinned release.
D=3 (011b) is not its own bit reversal (110b), S=1, and F=33 has bits 0 and 5 set, so a reversed bit order in D or F, or a misplaced S, cannot pass. A render of the pinned release.

The signal of IrpTransmogrifierNGTest.testDecodeRecs80Junk (L333-L336 @ c945e76): eleven exact durations asserted to decode as RECS80 {D=6,F=56,T=1}. That assertion is published; this Pronto string is not, so it is a render of the pinned release, and tests/test_recs80.py separately checks this encoder reproduces the published microsecond durations exactly.

The parameters of the second published decode assertion (testDecodeRecs80Multiple, L348-L351: a capture whose frames decode to D=2,F=1 with T=1 then T=0), in the T=0 state a remote file carries. A render of the pinned release.

RECS80-0068 has no published vector of its own; this is a render of the pinned release at the parameters of the published RECS80 assertion. Our bytes differ from the tool's at every space word but one: at 33.3 kHz the Pronto frequency word is 124, which plays at 33.46 kHz, and D6 rule 4 measures against that period where IrpTransmogrifier measures against 33.3 kHz.
As above at the second assertion's parameters and T=0. Differs from our bytes at the same words, for the same reason (the 33.3 kHz word truncates to 124).
